lesson.title: Governing Without a Playbook
lesson.summary: George Washington, unanimously elected the nation's first president in 1789, spent his two terms establishing precedents, from the cabinet system to the two-term tradition, for a constitutional government that had never actually been run before.
lesson.body:
When George Washington took the oath of office on April 30, 1789, in New York City, he was stepping into a role that existed on paper, in the Constitution the Philadelphia convention had produced two years earlier, but had never actually been performed by anyone. The Constitutional Convention that Washington had presided over had designed the presidency in fairly general terms, trusting in part that Washington himself, whose personal restraint and evident lack of interest in kingly power reassured even skeptics, would fill the office responsibly. The Electoral College chose him unanimously, an outcome that would repeat when he was reelected in 1792 and that no other president has matched since.

Washington understood, perhaps more clearly than anyone else at the time, that nearly everything he did would become precedent for those who followed him. He built the first cabinet by appointing leading figures to head executive departments, including Alexander Hamilton as Secretary of the Treasury, Thomas Jefferson as Secretary of State, Henry Knox as Secretary of War, and Edmund Randolph as Attorney General, creating an advisory body the Constitution had not explicitly required but that became a permanent fixture of the presidency. He also worked with Congress to pass the Judiciary Act of 1789, which established the federal court system, including the Supreme Court and lower federal courts, filling in structure the Constitution had only sketched.

His presidency also had to answer questions the peace at the Treaty of Paris had left unresolved. British troops still lingered at forts in the Northwest Territory, and tensions with both Britain and revolutionary France tested Washington's judgment repeatedly; in 1793 he issued a Neutrality Proclamation to keep the young nation out of the widening European war rather than be pulled in by either former ally or former enemy. At home, when farmers in western Pennsylvania violently resisted a federal excise tax on whiskey in 1794, Washington personally led militia forces into the field, a forceful demonstration that the new federal government, unlike the one under the Articles of Confederation, could and would enforce its own laws.

Perhaps his most lasting precedent was choosing to step down. After two terms, with no constitutional requirement forcing him to leave and considerable public sentiment that might have supported a third term, Washington voluntarily retired in 1797, establishing an informal two-term tradition that would hold, with one twentieth century exception, until it was formally written into the Constitution as the Twenty-Second Amendment more than a century and a half later.

Washington's cabinet also became the incubator for the deepest political rivalry of the early republic, as Hamilton's expansive vision of federal power repeatedly clashed with Jefferson's more cautious one, a conflict that would shape the nation's first political parties and that Hamilton, fresh off co-authoring the Federalist Papers, was determined to win.
